lessons.title: Who your customers are and what they expect
lessons.html:
Who your customers are

In grain handling and meat inspection, customers are not only people who buy. A customer is anyone who receives your service or product.

  • External customers: farmers delivering grain to the silo, traders and millers collecting grain, transporters, butchers and retailers buying carcasses, members of the public.
  • Internal customers: other departments that depend on your work. The weighbridge serves the grading office; the grader serves the bin manager; the meat inspector's decisions affect the abattoir's slaughter line and dispatch.

What customers expect

  • Reliability: doing what was promised, every time. A grade or a mass recorded correctly.
  • Responsiveness: prompt service. A farmer's truck waiting three hours at intake in harvest season costs him money and goodwill.
  • Competence: staff who know the grading rules, the procedures and the product.
  • Courtesy and respect: greeting people, listening, using their name, speaking a language they understand where possible.
  • Clear information: explaining grades, deductions, inspection outcomes and fees in plain words.
  • Fairness: the same rules applied to everyone, large commercial farmer or small-scale producer.

Service standards

Good organisations set service standards so staff know what is expected, for example: greet every driver at the weighbridge within two minutes; issue weighbridge tickets with no errors; return phone calls the same working day; resolve complaints within an agreed number of days. As a level 4 worker or supervisor you help set, communicate and monitor these standards.

Why it matters

In a competitive grain market a farmer can deliver to another silo. A butcher can buy from another abattoir. Poor service loses business; good service builds loyalty and a good name in the district, which in farming communities travels fast.

lessons.title: Communicating, solving problems and handling complaints
lessons.html:
Communicating with customers

  • Greet the customer and introduce yourself.
  • Listen actively: let the person finish, ask questions to understand, repeat back the main point.
  • Watch body language and tone, yours and theirs.
  • Explain decisions with facts. For example: the sample had foreign matter above the limit for that grade, so it was graded lower. Show the result sheet.
  • Do not promise what you cannot deliver.
  • On the phone and by message, be polite, clear and brief, and confirm agreements in writing.

Handling complaints

A complaint is a chance to fix a problem and keep the customer. Use a simple process:

  1. Listen without interrupting or arguing.
  2. Acknowledge the person's feelings: I understand this delay is costing you.
  3. Get the facts: ticket number, date, mass, grade, what happened.
  4. Act within your authority, or refer it to the person who can, and tell the customer who and when.
  5. Follow up to make sure the solution worked.
  6. Record the complaint and the outcome in the complaints register.

Example

A farmer disputes a grade on his sorghum delivery. The grader stays calm, shows him the sample, explains each deduction, and offers a re-test of the retained sample by the senior grader, as allowed by the silo's procedure. The re-test confirms the grade. The farmer is not happy with the price but accepts that the process was fair and open.

Difficult customers

  • Stay calm and polite, do not take it personally.
  • Never shout back or use bad language.
  • If a person becomes threatening, step away and call your supervisor or security.

Improving service

Review complaints and compliments regularly. Look for patterns: are waiting times always long on Mondays? Are certain grades often disputed? Fix the cause, not just the single case. Share lessons with the team.

Key points

  • Customers can be external or internal.
  • Customers expect reliability, responsiveness, competence, courtesy, clear information and fairness.
  • Listen actively and explain decisions with facts.
  • Handle complaints by listening, acknowledging, getting facts, acting, following up and recording.
  • Use complaint patterns to improve the service.

quiz.question: Which of these is an internal customer?

options.text: The grading office that depends on the weighbridge

quiz.question: A farmer disputes a grade. What is the best first response?

options.text: Tell him the grade is final and walk away
Listen, show the sample and explain the deductions with facts
Change the grade to keep him happy
Preparing your answer while they talk
Repeating back the main point to check understanding

quiz.question: Why should complaints be recorded in a register?

options.text: So patterns can be found and causes fixed
